item.title: Bangladesh launches national platform to tackle plastic pollution
item.description:
Bangladesh has launched the National Plastic Action Partnership (NPAP) to strengthen coordination among government agencies, businesses, development partners and civil society in tackling plastic pollution and accelerating the transition to a circular economy.
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo inaugurated the initiative at a national conference in Dhaka on Tuesday, calling for stronger coordination and effective implementation of plastic waste management policies.
The partnership brings together the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, the Department of Environment (DoE), UNDP Bangladesh and the World Economic Forum’s Global Plastic Action Partnership (GPAP).
Speaking as chief guest, Mintoo said plastic pollution threatens public health and ecosystems across cities, rivers, wetlands and coastal areas, while plastic production and consumption remain closely linked to trade, employment and economic activities.
“Today is an important moment as we move from recognizing the challenges of plastic pollution towards building stronger systems to address them,” he said.
Mintoo stressed that tackling plastic pollution requires action across the entire plastics value chain, from production and consumption to collection, reuse and recycling.
A circular economy could reduce unnecessary plastic use, extend the life of materials and keep valuable resources in circulation for longer, creating environmental, social and economic benefits, he said.
The minister highlighted the government's Guidelines for Plastic Waste Management 2026, which establish responsibilities for manufacturers, importers and brand owners in collecting and recycling plastic waste.
Under the guidelines, producers can fulfil their obligations individually or collectively through producer responsibility organisations.
Mintoo said effective enforcement would depend on reliable data, cooperation among stakeholders, adequate collection and recycling infrastructure, functioning markets, transparency and accountability.
“Policies achieve their purpose only when they can be implemented effectively,” he said, emphasizing the need for collaboration among producers, regulators, researchers and local authorities.
He said Bangladesh already had various institutions working on plastic waste management, adding that the NPAP would help coordinate existing initiatives, address information gaps and connect policy commitments with implementation and investment.
The minister urged businesses to develop innovative materials and industrial solutions, universities and research institutions to strengthen the evidence base, and development partners to align their support with national priorities.
He also called on financial institutions to explore investment opportunities in circular economy businesses and urged civil society organizations to ensure community voices were represented in decision-making.
Highlighting the contribution of waste collectors, sorters and recyclers, Mintoo said their practical experiences and livelihood concerns must be considered in shaping policies.
He added that the partnership's success should be assessed through measurable improvements in policy implementation, investment, recycling, practical solutions and working conditions in the waste sector, rather than the number of meetings held.
The conference, held under the theme “Unifying Action to Move to a Circular Economy”, brought together around 150 representatives from government agencies, businesses, development organisations, academia, research institutions, civil society and the waste management sector.
The partnership is intended to provide a coordinated framework for addressing gaps in plastic waste management and strengthening accountability across the plastics value chain.
By bringing public and private stakeholders together, the initiative aims to promote evidence-based policymaking, expand recycling opportunities and encourage investment in sustainable waste management.

item.title: Economic growth to slow, inflation to rise, putting people under greater pressure
item.description:
Bangladesh’s economy could grow more slowly than those of other South Asian countries, while inflationary pressure is likely to remain the highest in the region.

According to forecasts by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Bangladesh’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth could fall to 3.2 per cent in the current fiscal year, while average annual inflation could reach 10.9 per cent.

There is little indication of a strong economic recovery over the next few years. The IMF expects growth to fall further, to 2.2 per cent in the following fiscal year. On Tuesday, the organisation published its World Economic Outlook, which included GDP growth and inflation forecasts for Bangladesh and other countries.

Sluggish growth will put further pressure on investment and employment, while high inflation will erode people’s purchasing power. The World Bank recently reported that around eight million people had fallen below the poverty line over the past four years. Approximately 62.5 million people in Bangladesh are at risk of falling into poverty.

Official figures put growth at 4.14 per cent in the previous fiscal year. If the IMF’s forecast for the current fiscal year proves accurate, Bangladesh will not have recorded such a low growth rate in the past three and a half decades. Its inflation forecast would also imply the highest average annual inflation in 15 years.

The strain caused by economic weakness is therefore not confined to growth figures; it is directly affecting people’s living standards. Weakness in the banking sector, energy shortages, stagnant private investment and shortfalls in revenue collection are making the situation more complicated. Taken together, these factors are fuelling concerns about economic recovery, job creation and people’s quality of life.

The IMF is not alone in projecting relatively weak growth. The World Bank and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) have also issued modest forecasts. The World Bank’s Bangladesh Development Update, published on 6 September, projected growth of 3.4 per cent in the current fiscal year.

Inflation may rise to nearly 11pc this fiscal year, IMF forecasts

Last month, the ADB forecast growth of 4 per cent. The IMF’s projection is lower than both. The government, however, has set a growth target of 6.5 per cent for the current fiscal year.

Official figures put growth at 4.14 per cent in the previous fiscal year. If the IMF’s forecast for the current fiscal year proves accurate, Bangladesh will not have recorded such a low growth rate in the past three and a half decades. Its inflation forecast would also imply the highest average annual inflation in 15 years.

The annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank are under way in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand. Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury met World Bank representatives there on Tuesday.

Asked after the meeting about the growth and inflation forecasts, he told journalists that the two institutions had issued their projections and that he did not want to dispute them. The government was working towards the targets set in the budget, he said.

Zahid Hussain, former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office, told Prothom Alo that, given the current trajectory of the economy, growth would be weak and inflation would rise to a high level.

Zahid Hussain, former Lead Economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka officeInflation must be brought under control and the obstacles to growth and job creation must be removed. These include a weak banking sector, energy shortages, disorderly budget management and inadequate social protection programmes. Reforms are needed in all these areas.

He further said the IMF, World Bank and other organisations were all saying that the country’s economy was going through a difficult period. Ordinary people were already under pressure, and that pressure would intensify. Inflation would reduce their purchasing power and push more people into poverty, he added.

IMF’s new $4.5b loan, deal may be signed in December

Growth could fall further

The IMF has issued forecasts for Bangladesh’s GDP growth and inflation, including projections for the next four fiscal years. According to its forecasts, growth could fall to 2.2 per cent in fiscal year 2027–28, below the rate recorded during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The IMF projects growth of 2.8 per cent and 2.9 per cent in the following two fiscal years, respectively, before it rises to 3 per cent in fiscal year 2030–31. In other words, the economy is unlikely to gain much momentum over the next three years.

In its report published on Tuesday, the IMF also provided growth and inflation forecasts for other South Asian countries, including India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. According to the report, India’s growth in fiscal year 2026–27 could reach 7 per cent, with inflation at 4.4 per cent. Pakistan’s growth is projected at 3.5 per cent.

The World Bank considers weakness in the banking sector one of the major risks facing Bangladesh’s economy. The non-performing loan ratio stood at 20.2 per cent at the end of December 2024. By June 2026, it had risen to 33.2 per cent.

Sri Lanka could record growth of 3.7 per cent and inflation of 5.4 per cent, while Nepal’s growth and inflation are projected at 3.7 per cent and 5.8 per cent, respectively. The Maldives could see growth of 3.8 per cent and inflation of 2.5 per cent, while Bhutan’s growth could reach 6.9 per cent, with inflation at 6.5 per cent.

What are the risks to the economy?

The IMF report did not provide an analysis of Bangladesh’s economy or discuss the challenges it faces. The World Bank, however, analysed the country’s economic situation in its Bangladesh Development Update, published on 6 September.

The World Bank report said several pressures were building up simultaneously. Economic growth was slowing, investment and employment were weakening, and inflation was reducing people’s real incomes. Weakness in the banking sector, energy shortages and revenue shortfalls were adding to the risks.

The World Bank identified weaknesses in the banking sector as one of the biggest threats to the economy.

The World Bank report further said poverty had increased because of factors including declining real incomes caused by high inflation and a slowdown in employment. Around eight million people had fallen below the poverty line over the past four years, while approximately 2.1 million more fell below it in the previous fiscal year alone.

According to the report, the national poverty rate has risen for four consecutive years, increasing from 18.7 per cent in 2022 to an estimated 22.5 per cent in the previous fiscal year. It could rise further to 22.8 per cent in the current fiscal year. Income inequality has also increased over the same period.

The World Bank considers weakness in the banking sector one of the major risks facing Bangladesh’s economy. The non-performing loan ratio stood at 20.2 per cent at the end of December 2024. By June 2026, it had risen to 33.2 per cent.

According to the World Bank, private-sector credit growth is at its lowest level in 33 years. Shortages of gas and electricity have forced many factories to operate below capacity. Some businesses have reduced working hours, suspended production or laid off workers. Foreign investment fell by 15 per cent last year.

The government has also had to spend several billion dollars more to import fuel. Meanwhile, revenue collection has made little progress. The National Board of Revenue (NBR) has been unable to meet its targets, with the revenue shortfall exceeding Tk 250 billion in the first two months of the fiscal year, July and August. These factors have combined to create mounting pressure on the economy.

Asked what should be done to overcome the situation, economist Zahid Hussain said inflation must be brought under control and the obstacles to growth and job creation must be removed.

These include a weak banking sector, energy shortages, disorderly budget management and inadequate social protection programmes. Reforms are needed in all these areas, he said.

item.title: Saudi coalition strikes Yemen oil sites after Houthi attacks
item.description:
YEMEN-SAUDI-IRAN-US-ISRAEL-WAR

The Saudi-led coalition battling the Iran-backed Houthis struck oil sites across western Yemen on Tuesday including in the capital Sanaa, in response to the deadliest attack on the kingdom’s soil in years.

Blasts were heard shortly after in Saudi capital Riyadh and at an oil giant Aramco facility in eastern Saudi Arabia, witnesses and journalists told AFP.

The coalition said it intercepted several Houthi missiles targeting the kingdom, including Riyadh, adding that debris fell in a residential area in Dhahran, which hosts Aramco’s headquarters.

Tuesday’s coalition strikes in Yemen’s Sanaa and the western provinces of Dhamar and Saada targeted facilities used to “supply the war effort” by the Houthis to “threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and waterways”, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote on X.

A powerful explosion then rang out in the Saudi capital, with a phone alert sent to residents saying “the city of Riyadh is facing a hostile aerial threat”.

While walking down a major avenue in Riyadh, a witness told AFP he “saw a projectile cutting across the sky” above a mall, saying it left “a yellowish trail of light followed by a trail of smoke. Then, we heard an explosion.”

“People were calm; no one was speaking. We were scared and all looking up at the sky,” he added, requesting anonymity.

After Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and energy sites in recent days, the coalition issued its first evacuation order in the Yemeni capital since the war flared in July, before attacking the Yemen Petroleum Company facility on Sanaa’s outskirts.

An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said “Saudi aggression” targeted the oil firm.

Renewed threats

A strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.

The Saudi cabinet vowed in a meeting earlier Tuesday, led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, that it “will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait to be threatened”.

An AFP correspondent reported that many civilians in Sanaa fearing shortages rushed to queue in front of fuel stations after the coalition warning.

The Houthis had earlier issued a new threat to target Riyadh’s international airport, a refinery, and an Aramco facility in Dammam if the strike went ahead, calling for citizens to avoid them.

Many countries have issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia, most recently France, which told its citizens to avoid Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam airports.

The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen’s government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a dire humanitarian crisis.

Economic woes

Traffic in perennially gridlocked Riyadh was noticeably lighter this week, as remote learning for all schools and work-from-home orders for some companies took effect, according to AFP journalists.

Saudi Arabia faces a major economic contraction this year with GDP expected to shrink 3.3 percent, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday, predicting a regional drop over Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

The kingdom was already facing headwinds from Iran’s chokehold on the Hormuz strait since the start of the Middle East war in February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran.

But the restart in July of Yemen’s frozen war has further roiled the kingdom and brought the fight to its own soil.

Houthi attacks have also targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea—Saudi Arabia’s alternative export route.

In Yemen, the renewed fighting was fuelling the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.

Suspected cholera cases tripled there in three weeks, the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating war casualties.

‘Behaving very badly’

The Riyadh airport attack had prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.

He wrote on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday that “the Houthis are behaving very badly”, accusing them of acting “probably at the behest of Iran”.

“I’ll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!” he wrote, referring to next month’s midterms.

The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti telling AFP they would target American interests in the region.

Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince “that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position”.

item.title: Washington should provide Dhaka with increased support amid rising imports: Finance Minister
item.description:
Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury today, Saturday said Bangladesh should receive increased support from the United States in view of improving bilateral relations and the country's growing imports from the US.

He made the remarks while briefing journalists after a meeting with officials of the US Treasury Department here today.

The meeting discussed debt management, US assistance and overall Bangladesh-US relations, the minister said. He also held discussions with representatives of the US Export-Import Bank (EXIM Bank) and other US agencies involved in providing assistance.

"Bangladesh did not receive much from the United States in the past. But, as Bangladesh-US relations have progressed, we are purchasing several aircraft and importing oil, soybeans and various other products and commodities from the US. Therefore, we should receive additional support from them. They agreed on this. Now, let us see," Amir Khosru said.

The finance minister said the government's economic policy prioritises reducing dependence on loans and increasing foreign direct investment (FDI) and joint investment.

Khosru said he had held extensive discussions with the US EXIM Bank on the issue and expressed hope that Bangladesh could move forward with this approach.

"The main focus of our economic policy is investment. We want to move away from loans and focus more on direct investment and joint investment," he said.

Highlighting Bangladesh's substantial imports from the United States, the minister said purchases of aircraft, oil, soybeans and other commodities had implications for bilateral trade as well as Bangladesh's external balance of payments.

"We have strongly told them that Bangladesh is importing so much from the United States, and bilateral relations have reached their current stage.

If support does not come from the US now, when will it come? The assistance we expect should come now," he said.

Amir Khosru said the relevant US parties agreed with Bangladesh's position. However, he added, the extent and modalities of the expected assistance would become clear in the coming days.

item.title: Bangladeshis sent to Russia for jobs, used as 'prey' in war, 20 killed: SRB
item.description:
Thirty Bangladeshis went to Russia in search of jobs after being promised employment at construction companies.

But upon arrival, their passports and mobile phones were confiscated, and they were handed over to the military.

After 21 days of military training, they were deployed to the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Special Response Battalion (SRB) has found that at least 20 Bangladeshis died in drone strikes there.

A preliminary SRB investigation found that the Bangladeshis were sent to the battlefield as a kind of bait to identify enemy positions.

When drones struck them, the attackers’ positions and distance could be determined.

Additional Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Md Asaduzzaman, commander of SRB-10 Battalion, disclosed the information at a press conference in Karwan Bazar in the capital on Wednesday.

Two people have been arrested in connection with the incident: Mizanur Rahman, 55, founder of Jabal-e-Noor International and one of the key figures in the human trafficking network, and Abu Taher, also known as Lentu.

According to the SRB, the 30 Bangladeshis travelled to Russia on 7 May this year through three companies: Jabal-e-Noor, RS International and TS Group. Each was charged an average of around Tk 1 million on the promise of construction jobs. However, instead of providing the promised employment, the recruiters handed them over to the Russian military after they arrived. They were then sent to the battlefield following 21 days of training.

“The people taken from Bangladesh were not fit for combat. They had no physical, military or tactical training suitable for warfare. So why were they deployed after just 21 days of training? What we have understood is that they were sent to the battlefield as a kind of bait to identify enemy positions. When the opposing side launches drone strikes against them, its positions can be identified,” Asaduzzaman said.

The SRB said the Bangladeshis were deployed in three zones of the battlefield: the front, middle and rear. Seventeen were killed in drone strikes on the very first day. Three more deaths were reported at different times later. The battalion has provisionally confirmed the deaths of 20 of the 30 Bangladeshis.

At the press conference, Asaduzzaman said two of the survivors had returned to Bangladesh with injuries. One of them, Rajan, said a drone strike on the battlefield broke his pelvis and left the lower half of his body paralysed. He managed to reach a camp by crawling on his chest for nearly four kilometres.

Of the remaining eight, two are receiving treatment at a hospital in Moscow, while the other six are still on the battlefield.

Asaduzzaman said the trafficking network involved not only Bangladeshis but also a Russian national named Igor and a Kyrgyz woman named Julia. Efforts are underway to gather information about them and conduct operations. The authorities are also trying to arrest another member of the network, Mostafizur.

The SRB official said preliminary findings suggested that people from several countries had been recruited in a similar manner to fight in Russia’s war. From Bangladesh, recruits had come particularly from Gopalganj, Mymensingh, Narayanganj, Jamalpur, Pabna, Chapainawabganj, Faridpur, Rajbari and Gazipur.

Asaduzzaman added that most of the victims came from poor families, and some had borrowed money to travel abroad. Many of their families have now received news of their loved ones’ deaths but have no opportunity to see the bodies or bring them home.

He urged people to exercise caution when offered overseas jobs, particularly when making payments to recruiters, and to verify the legitimacy of the companies involved before travelling.

item.title: Press Council seeks power to act suo motu and fine journalists
item.description:
The Bangladesh Press Council wants legal authority to act on its own initiative against the publication of news reports that it considers harmful to national integrity, independence or sovereignty, or detrimental to the public interest.

It also believes it should have the power to take similar action against the spread of rumours, fake news and hate speech. In addition, the council wants the law amended to allow it to impose financial penalties on journalists as a form of punishment.

These proposals are outlined in a report submitted by the Press Council to the parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The committee has yet to discuss the report.

Those familiar with the matter say the Bangladesh Press Council was established to safeguard press freedom and improve and maintain the standards of newspapers and news agencies.

However, the government body has rarely been seen playing a role in protecting press freedom. Instead, during the tenure of the ousted Awami League government, it drafted proposals to amend its governing law in ways that journalists described as an attempt to curtail press freedom.

The powers it is now seeking represent a revival of that earlier effort. Granting the council authority to initiate proceedings on its own would run counter to independent journalism and democratic practice, they argue.

According to sources familiar with the matter, one item on Tuesday’s agenda of the parliamentary standing committee was a discussion on how to make the activities of organisations under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting more dynamic and responsive to the public. In response, 14 organisations under the ministry submitted written proposals to the committee.

It states: “If newspapers, news agencies, editors, publishers or journalists publish or print news or reports that are harmful to the country’s national integrity, independence or sovereignty, contrary to public taste or journalistic codes of conduct, or detrimental to the public interest, or if they spread rumours, fake news or hate speech, the law should empower the council to initiate investigations, issue orders and take necessary action on its own initiative.”

One was titled “Specific proposals to make the overall activities of the Bangladesh Press Council more dynamic and public-oriented”. The report was signed by Press Council Secretary Md Abdus Sabur, a joint secretary of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

The Press Council’s proposal states that the Press Council Act, enacted in the context of 1974, urgently needs to be updated to keep pace with the current era of free-flowing information and the rapid expansion of modern, technology-driven media.

The aim, it says, is to protect press freedom, improve and maintain media standards, and prevent malpractice in journalism and disinformation. To achieve this, the law should incorporate additional powers and areas of jurisdiction. The proposal lists 19 such powers.

They include registering journalists and issuing them certificates, setting minimum educational qualifications, bringing online news outlets under the council’s jurisdiction, establishing a code of conduct for journalists, and investigating attacks on or obstruction of independent journalism while providing protection to those affected.

The council also proposes that it be authorised to collect a levy or contribution from newspapers based on their circulation to ensure its financial self-sufficiency.

The Press Council Act was also slated for amendment under the Awami League government, which was ousted in the July mass uprising. In June 2022, the Cabinet gave in-principle approval to a draft amendment. The law was ultimately not amended.

NOAB President and Manabzamin chief editor Matiur Rahman ChowdhuryIf the Press Council or any other institution were given the power to act on its own initiative, there would be little need for the courts and the legal process.

At the time, the proposed changes included financial penalties and the power to take cognisance of offences on the council’s own initiative. The draft initially proposed fines of up to Tk 1 million, but the specific amount was removed when the Cabinet granted its in-principle approval.

The initiative drew criticism during the Awami League’s tenure. The Newspaper Owners’ Association of Bangladesh (NOAB) objected to the proposals, saying, “The proposed amendments are vague and therefore open to abuse. In particular, they refer to matters harmful to or derogatory towards the security, independence and sovereignty of the state, but provide no precise interpretation of these terms.”

Asked about the Press Council’s proposals to the parliamentary standing committee, NOAB President and Manabzamin chief editor Matiur Rahman Chowdhury told Prothom Alo that if the Press Council or any other institution were given the power to act on its own initiative, there would be little need for the courts and the legal process.

The way these legal powers are being proposed would obstruct democratic practice and independent journalism, he said. Attempts were made to introduce similar provisions under the Awami League government. It would be unfortunate if the same effort were repeated now.

He added that the council was unable to exercise even the powers it already possessed. Many people regarded it as a toothless institution, he said, and any amendment to the law must be preceded by consultations with stakeholders.

In what circumstances does the council want to investigate on its own initiative?

The report says the Press Council should be empowered to initiate investigations and take appropriate action in certain circumstances.

It states: “If newspapers, news agencies, editors, publishers or journalists publish or print news or reports that are harmful to the country’s national integrity, independence or sovereignty, contrary to public taste or journalistic codes of conduct, or detrimental to the public interest, or if they spread rumours, fake news or hate speech, the law should empower the council to initiate investigations, issue orders and take necessary action on its own initiative.”

The report further says the council should be authorised to investigate and order necessary protective measures when the freedom to publish news or practise independent journalism is obstructed, or when journalists face attacks or mob violence.

Such action could follow a complaint by the publisher or editor of an affected newspaper, or be initiated by the council itself when there are credible grounds to believe that press freedom has been violated.

The council has also proposed a provision to expedite the resolution of complaints. Under the proposed procedure, when an aggrieved person files a complaint, the council would initially direct the editor of the newspaper concerned to resolve the matter. The editor would then discuss the complaint with the complainant and seek a settlement.

The Press Council currently operates as a quasi-judicial body. It says a judge of district judge rank should be included as a member and that the council should be given exclusive authority to adjudicate matters involving journalists’ rights and professional misconduct.

The report also proposes effective legal provisions allowing financial penalties for publishing false or harassing reports, material that violates journalistic ethics or public taste, or content that breaches the code of conduct.

Emphasising the need for a code of conduct for journalists, the proposal argues that, because compliance is not mandatory, journalists are not sufficiently conscious of the need to uphold professional ethics, publish objective news and practise responsible journalism. It therefore recommends adding a provision requiring the code to be published in the official gazette. The council itself would draft the code.

The report also takes issue with journalists working in other professions simultaneously. It describes this as a clear violation of journalistic principles and ethics and a serious form of professional misconduct.

Holding two or more jobs at the same time, it argues, undermines the professional standards and dignity of journalism. The council says this restriction should be explicitly incorporated into the law.

Former head of the Media Reform Commission Kamal Ahmed, asked about the proposals, said there appeared to be a misconception that the Press Council was a judicial institution. It is an organisation under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, he said, and should not be granted the power to issue orders on its own initiative.

He also noted that the proposal did not address bringing broadcast media under the Press Council’s jurisdiction. “Will a separate authority be established for that purpose?” he asked.

Kamal Ahmed said the current government should adopt the proposals made by the Media Reform Commission. Instead, the latest proposals selectively retain certain elements, he argued.

Kamal Ahmed further said that reviving an ineffective institution such as the Press Council in this way would not benefit the media. Rather, it should be abolished and replaced with the commission promised by the BNP, he said, a body that would be independent and permanent.

item.title: 2 major Bangladeshi conglomerates to begin lithium-ion battery production
item.description:
Demand for lithium-ion batteries is rising in Bangladesh as the use of electric vehicles and renewable energy continues to grow. Seeking to tap into this expanding market, two of the country’s major industrial groups, Walton and PRAN-RFL, have invested in the sector.

Walton will begin producing lithium-ion battery cells next month, while PRAN-RFL Group plans to import lithium-ion cells and manufacture battery packs at its own factory in November.

Walton Hi-Tech Industries, a subsidiary of Walton Group, has established a lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing plant in Chandra, Gazipur.

The factory will have an annual production capacity of 10 million (1 crore) battery cells. These cells will be used in products such as motorcycles, toys, rechargeable lights, rechargeable fans and digital scales. The company has invested Tk 1.13 billion (113 crore) in the project so far.

PRAN-RFL Group has established a lithium-ion battery pack manufacturing plant at its industrial park in Habiganj.

The facility will have an annual production capacity of 60,000 battery packs. The company has already invested Tk 250 million (25 crore) in the project.

Bangladesh’s annual market for all types of batteries is currently worth around Tk 150 billion.

Lithium-ion batteries account for Tk 20 billion to Tk 25 billion of this market. This means lead-acid batteries still dominate the sector. However, companies investing in the industry expect lithium-ion batteries to gradually replace lead-acid batteries.

Discussions with industry insiders reveal that demand for batteries is growing rapidly for battery-powered rickshaws, electric bikes and electricity storage in homes, commercial establishments and industrial facilities.

Bangladesh currently has an estimated 150,000 battery-powered rickshaws. The annual market for batteries used in this sector is worth between Tk 16 billion and Tk 18 billion.

Meanwhile, 12,000 to 16,000 electric two-wheelers, or electric bikes, are sold annually. The batteries used in these vehicles represent an annual market worth Tk 6.75 billion to Tk 9 billion.

In addition, batteries used for electricity storage account for an annual market worth Tk 9 billion. Companies entering the sector are targeting these three markets with their investments.

Industry insiders say lithium-ion batteries are lighter and more durable than conventional lead-acid batteries. They also charge in approximately one-third of the time required by lead-acid batteries, making them more energy-efficient. However, lithium-ion batteries cost nearly twice as much as conventional lead-acid batteries.

Walton to manufacture battery cells

Walton officials said the company would soon begin producing large prismatic lithium and sodium battery cells for battery-powered auto-rickshaws and solar energy storage systems. The initiative will require an additional investment of Tk 4 billion to Tk 5 billion.

Mahfuzur Rahman, chief business officer (CBO) of the lithium-ion battery project at Walton Hi-Tech Industries, told Prothom Alo that the company had completed the commissioning of the equipment installed to manufacture lithium-ion battery cells.

Trial production will begin this month or next month. The company also plans to launch lithium and sodium battery pack production lines within the next three to four months.

Mahfuzur Rahman added, “Using these production lines, we will begin manufacturing large batteries for easy-bikes, telecommunications equipment, IPS and UPS systems, solar energy storage, cars, electric bikes, forklifts and other applications.”

PRAN-RFL to manufacture battery packs

PRAN-RFL Group, one of Bangladesh’s leading industrial conglomerates, will begin manufacturing lithium-ion battery packs at its industrial park in Habiganj next month using imported cells.

Initially, the company will import lithium cells, along with certain specialised electronic components and other materials, from abroad.

As a result, local value addition in lithium-ion battery pack production will initially stand at around 20 per cent.

However, several senior officials of the group said it planned to increase local value addition to 70–80 per cent by expanding its own manufacturing facilities in the future.

PRAN-RFL Group said it would initially manufacture various types of lithium-ion batteries for easy-bikes, mishuks and electric bikes. The group will market these batteries under its own Blaze brand.

Asked about future plans, Kazi Rashedul Islam, deputy general manager of the RFL Batteries and Cables project, said, “We also plan to manufacture batteries for solar energy storage systems, IPS and UPS systems, backup power systems in the telecommunications sector, and energy storage at industrial facilities.”

He said the company planned to invest an additional Tk 1 billion (100 crore) next year to expand its lithium-ion battery manufacturing plant.

The lithium-ion battery plant of PRAN-RFL Group will initially create employment for 300 people. The company expects to generate jobs for another 500 people next year.

Although the group will initially manufacture lithium-ion batteries for the domestic market, it plans to export lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries in the future.

RN Paul, managing director (MD) of RFL Group, said, “Demand for lithium-ion batteries in Bangladesh has so far been met mainly through imports. In particular, finished batteries and the necessary components are imported from China. Once local production begins, imports of finished batteries will decline. This will save a substantial amount of foreign currency.”

item.title: Cabinet body recommends procurement of LNG from 5 suppliers
item.description:
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs on Wednesday recommended approval in principle for procuring liquefied natural gas (LNG) from five international suppliers through government-to-government (G2G) and direct procurement methods to help maintain an uninterrupted gas supply in the country.
The recommendations were made at a meeting of the committee held with Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury in the chair.
The Energy and Mineral Resources Division placed two proposals, seeking approval for LNG procurement under the Public Procurement Act, 2006, and the Public Procurement Rules, 2025.
Under the first proposal, the committee recommended approval in principle to process proposals submitted by Cheniere Marketing International LLP and Trafigura Pte Ltd for LNG supply through the G2G method.
The proposal was processed under Section 68 of the Public Procurement Act, 2006, and Rules 99(2) and 107(2) of the Public Procurement Rules, 2025.
The second proposal sought approval to purchase LNG directly from BP Singapore Pte Limited, Sahara Energy Resource Limited and Shell International Trading Middle East Limited FZE.
The Energy and Mineral Resources Division cited the urgent need to maintain normal gas supplies in the national interest as the basis for the proposed direct procurement.
The proposal was brought under Section 68 of the Public Procurement Act, 2006, and Rules 107, 97 and 98 of the Public Procurement Rules, 2025.
The committee recommended approval for the second proposal as well.
The recommendations are intended to facilitate the procurement process for LNG from the five suppliers. However, the proposals did not specify the volumes of LNG to be purchased, contract values or delivery schedules.

item.title: Bangladesh calls for global treaty to protect victims of crimes against humanity
item.description:
Bangladesh has called for a strong international convention to prevent and punish crimes against humanity, urging special recognition and support for countries hosting victims of such atrocities.
Addressing the Sixth Committee of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Bangladesh delegate Muhammad Nawshad Zamir proposed three key provisions for the convention: cooperation in preserving evidence and protecting witnesses in receiving States; support for survivors, including access to justice at national and international levels; and international solidarity in sharing the burden borne by host countries.
Citing Bangladesh’s experience sheltering over 1 million Rohingyas forcibly displaced from Myanmar, he stressed that countries receiving victims must be integral to international accountability mechanisms, according to the Permanent Mission of Bangladesh to the United Nations in New York.
Referring to Bangladesh’s 2024 uprising, Zamir cited a UN report estimating that up to 1,400 people, including children, were killed, calling for investigations into possible crimes against humanity.
Bangladesh also advocated universal jurisdiction, stronger extradition mechanisms and an end to impunity, while emphasising prevention and justice for women and children.
The Bangladesh delegate urged that the convention complement the Rome Statute and uphold the International Criminal Court’s independence.
“A convention diluted until it offends no one will protect no one,” he warned.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 5th globally in air pollution
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 5th among the world's most polluted cities on Wednesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 175 at 10:20am.
The air quality was classified as "unhealthy", meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
Singapore in Singapore ranked first with an AQI score of 194, while Delhi in India ranked second with a score of 180, followed by Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia in third place with an AQI score of 177.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered 'unhealthy for sensitive groups', while 151 to 200 is classified as 'unhealthy'. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered 'very unhealthy', while levels above 301 are deemed 'hazardous', posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: CCGP approves Tk 765.65C variations in 2 HSIA expansion contracts
item.description:
The Cabinet Committee on Government Purchase (CCGP) on Wednesday approved variations worth Tk765.65 crore in two contracts for the Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (HSIA) Expansion Project, including construction works and consultancy services.
The committee gave the approval at its meeting held with Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury in the chair.
The committee recommended a variation of Tk360.65 crore in the construction contract for the project’s first phase, third revised version, raising the contract value by 1.75% from Tk20,598.65 crore to Tk20,959.30 crore.
The construction contract was awarded to Aviation Dhaka Consortium (ADC), a joint venture comprising Japan’s Mitsubishi Corporation and Fujita Corporation and South Korea’s Samsung C&T.
The committee also recommended approving a Tk405 crore variation in the consultancy services contract for the same project.
The consultancy contract value will rise by 52.48% from Tk771.72 crore to Tk1,176.72 crore following the proposed variation.
The consultancy services are being provided by a joint venture comprising Japan’s Nippon Koei Co Ltd and Oriental Consultants Global Co Ltd, Singapore’s CPG Consultants Pte Ltd and Bangladesh’s Development Design Consultants Ltd.
Both proposals were placed by the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism.
The airport expansion project is aimed at improving the country’s main international airport facilities and handling capacity.

item.title: Pope Leo has cancerous tumour removed in lung operation
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous tumour removed from his right lung in a 90-minute operation on Tuesday and "woke up normally" after the procedure, the Vatican said.
A Vatican source said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread.
"To ensure the procedure was radical, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed," the Vatican said in a statement.
The operation "confirmed the diagnosis of a pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the pre-operative tests", it said.
The 71-year-old pope was in the operating room at Rome's Gemelli hospital for a total of three hours and the operation lasted half that time.
"The surgery was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said, with a source adding that he had requested dinner after the procedure.
Juanita Mora, medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association, told AFP that when this type of cancer is "caught in early stages, then it has a very, very good prognosis".
She said much would depend on the stage of the cancer found and whether it had spread.
In cases of surgical removal and when the cancer is caught early and localised, five-year survival rates from lung adenocarcinoma were "80 to 98 percent", she said.
"They'll determine if he needs chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy for the adenocarcinoma," she said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a practicing Catholic, said after the surgery that he and his wife were "united in prayer for (Leo's) health following his recent diagnosis".
"May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father," Rubio said on X.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his "thoughts and prayers" were with the pontiff, calling him "a voice for peace, humanity and reason in our modern world".
Leo had entered the hospital smiling and waving earlier on Tuesday hours before the surgery.
He is staying in a room on the 10th floor of the building, next to a papal suite with a private chapel that is currently under renovation.
The Vatican has said it expects the recovery to take a week.
His audiences have been cancelled until October 20 and the operation raises questions about whether the pope will go on a lengthy visit to Latin America next month.
The surgery marks Leo's first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025.
In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in St Peter's Square that doctors had discovered a nodule "at a very early stage" during medical checks.
"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene," he said.
The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo's predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments.
Ahead of the operation, people outside the hospital expressed concern over the pope's condition.
Giorgia Fei, a 57-year-old Italian, said she had been worried.
"However, the Holy Father is in very good hands here at the hospital because we have some outstanding doctors," she said.
"I will pray a lot for him."
Giuseppe Purpura, 72, said he too was concerned.
"He's still quite young and I really wasn't expecting this. I thought he was in better health," he said, noting that "thankfully it was caught in time".
The Vicar General for the Diocese of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, led a rosary prayer for the pope inside the hospital chapel which was broadcast by the Vatican.
Dozens of people attended, and Reina asked all the city's parishes to join in.
The Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told ANSA news agency that Leo had been "very calm" about his condition when they met on Monday.
The Vatican told AFP the nodule was found during routine health checks, and there were no symptoms that led to checking the pope's lungs.
Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and believed to generally be in good health.
He is scheduled to travel to South America from November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

item.title: Govt for ‘unprecedented cooperation’ with China, looks beyond infra projects: Shama Obaed
Budhi Gandaki flood poses no direct threat to Bangladesh, but it holds lessons for early warning
item.description:
Nepal has experienced two major floods within a short span of time. The flood in August was particularly devastating. The most recent one occurred on 11 October.

Such disasters in the Himalayan foothills are a warning not only for Nepal but also for other South Asian countries. Saswata Sanyal, intervention manager in ICIMOD’s Disaster Risk Reduction Division, spoke to Prothom Alo about the causes of the floods, early warning systems and the lessons the region can learn. The interview was conducted by Partha Shankar Saha.

Two major floods have hit Nepal within a relatively short period. Such disasters have long occurred because of the geological characteristics of the Himalayas. How can we determine whether climate warming is increasing the frequency or intensity of these floods? What evidence can help establish this?

Saswata Sanyal: The Himalayas are a relatively young mountain range with steep slopes and high seismic activity and they have a long history of both types of disasters. The same Bhotekoshi corridor was hit in July 2025. At that time, NDRRMA reported a glacial lake outburst originating in the upper catchment.

The two events in 2026 also had different causes. The Rasuwa–Gyirong flood in August began with a high-altitude rock–ice collapse. In the case of the Budhi Gandaki River flood, the NDRRMA has said provisionally that a landslide blocked the flow of a tributary. The dam later broke, triggering the flood. No link between this event and glaciers or ice has yet been established.

Warming primarily increases risks in high mountain areas through glacier thinning, permafrost thaw and increased meltwater. To distinguish these effects from geological hazards, several types of evidence are needed:

  • Using previous satellite data to compile a record of disasters over several decades, while correcting for gaps and biases in data collection;

  • Regularly measuring changes in land and glacier elevation in the same areas, and monitoring landslide-prone slopes and glaciers using radar-based InSAR technology;

  • Temperature and permafrost records at source elevations;

  • Rather than directly attributing an individual disaster to climate change, examining the relationship between warming and the hazardous conditions that developed before the event.

Another reason for the increase in damage is the growth of settlements, roads and hydropower plants along river valleys. As a result, the number of people living in vulnerable areas and the amount of infrastructure exposed to these hazards have also increased.

Reports say residents began warning one another around 4:45 am, while the first official warning came later and mass SMS alerts were sent at 6:40 am. What failed in the official warning chain, and how can community reports be incorporated quickly into a trusted, formal alert system?

Saswata Sanyal: On 11 October, residents began alerting one another at about 4:45 am. The Arughat police post issued the first official warning at 5:30 am. FFD and NDRRMA received initial reports around 6:00 am and sent mass SMS at 6:40 am. The nearest automatic water-level sensor is at Arughat, about 65 km downstream of the source, so the FFD relied on reports from residents and officials.

Once the warning system was activated, the dissemination of alerts worked properly. The question is not what failed, but it was to verify the detection, and the hand-off from a credible field report to an authorised alert. The idea is to not give false alerts from the government as well.

In remote mountain valleys with limited monitoring, what combination of local phone networks, river sensors, satellite observation and other tools could provide useful warning time for both landslide-dam outburst floods and glacial lake outburst floods?

Saswata Sanyal: Warning time comes from detecting the hazard high in the catchment and acting fast. A layered system works best:

  • Satellite screening: identifies growing lakes, slope creep and new landslide dams weeks to months ahead;

  • Seismic detection: flags large collapses within minutes;

  • Upstream network of sensors: placed at known glacial lakes and at newly formed dams once detected a network of different kind of sensors like cameras, microphone, geophones, wire sensors to focus on where exactly the breach is;

  • Trigger mechanism and sacrificial infrastructure: Rate of rise of water takes place faster than the data is transmitted to the server. Therefore, rate-of-rise can’t be captured. Additionally, if the sensors stop transmitting that should also trigger alerts as it means they have been washed away. On 11th Oct we saw the water level drop as well uncharacteristically, this should also trigger alerts as it mean that there might have been a major landslide upstream. The trigger mechanism needs to be overhauled;

  • Trained phone observers with satellite or radio backup: for when mobile towers fail.

Glacial lakes are largely known sites and can be instrumented. Landslide dams appear without notice, so they need rapid detection.

The flood damaged homes, bridges, trails and a hydropower construction site. Do current planning and engineering rules adequately account for fast-moving water carrying mud, rocks and debris? What changes are most urgent in the siting and protection of settlements and infrastructure?

Saswata Sanyal: Not adequately for these kind of impact or hazards. Infrastructure is typically designed for clear-water floods of a given return period. The government RDNA puts recovery needs at about USD 4.74 billion, around 75 per cent of it for infrastructure. Most urgent changes:

  • Multi-hazard risk informed land-use zoning to guide reconstruction, so recovery funds do not rebuild exposure;

  • Relocating construction camps, worker housing and border posts off valley floors;

  • Checking critical assets against debris-flow and outburst scenarios;

  • hydropower licence conditions covering upstream multi-hazard risk monitoring and evacuation plans;

  • Debris-tolerant river crossings.

For readers in Bangladesh, how should the Budhi Gandaki flood’s significance be understood? Is there any direct downstream concern beyond Nepal, or are the main lessons for Bangladesh about preparedness, monitoring and cooperation across Himalayan river basins?

Saswata Sanyal: There is no direct physical threat to Bangladesh. The Budhi Gandaki joins the Trishuli, which flows into the Narayani/Gandak and then the Ganges. Even the much larger August flood had attenuated to a routine level by Devghat in southern Nepal.

The relevance for Bangladesh lies in the lessons from Nepal’s gaps in detection, warning and planning:

  • Layered warning systems for fast-onset floods, combining satellite screening, seismic detection and upstream sensors, rather than relying only on downstream gauges designed for slow, rainfall-driven rises;

  • Alert triggers that respond to a sharp rate of rise, an unusual drop in water level or sensors going offline, not only to fixed danger levels;

  • A fast, verified hand-off from community reports to official alerts, where Bangladesh’s Cyclone Preparedness Programme is itself a model for the region;

  • Multi-hazard, risk-informed siting and design of riverside settlements, embankments and crossings, so that reconstruction does not rebuild exposure;

  • Timely, real-time upstream hydrological data, alongside longer-term research on sediment pulses moving through shared river systems.

These are shared risks across the Hindu Kush Himalaya. Data-sharing arrangements are for governments to agree, with common standards developed regionally.

Based on the recent floods, what are the three most urgent steps Nepal and regional agencies should take before the next high-impact event—and who needs to lead each step?

Saswata Sanyal: Drawing on the lessons above, three steps stand out:

Warning: a national alert-to-action protocol that links each warning level to fixed duties for every tier of government and every actor on a river, with a fast, verified route from community and field reports to pre-authorised alerts. Lead: NDRRMA, with DHM/FFD and local governments.

Detection: satellite screening of glacial lakes, unstable slopes and new landslide dams, starting with the most exposed river corridors, backed by upstream sensors and alert triggers that respond to rate of rise, sudden drops in water level and sensors going offline. Lead: DHM with universities and research institutes; ICIMOD supporting methods, regional data and training.

Planning and cooperation: multi-hazard, risk-informed zoning to guide reconstruction, debris-flow and outburst checks on critical assets, and hydropower licence conditions covering upstream multi-hazard monitoring and evacuation plans, alongside corridor-based data-sharing and warning arrangements with neighbouring countries. Lead: NDRRMA and local governments for zoning; the Department of Electricity Development for hydropower licences; governments through bilateral mechanisms for information-sharing, with ICIMOD and WMO supporting regional standards and platforms.

item.title: Parliamentary committee asks govt to identify officials obstructing its work
item.description:
A parliamentary committee has recommended that the Ministry of Public Administration identify and take necessary action against those obstructing or neglecting the current government’s activities aimed at implementing the policy of “Bangladesh first”.

The recommendation was made at a meeting of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Public Administration at the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban on Wednesday. The committee also recommended investigating the projects which were progressing slowly.

The information was disclosed in a press release issued by the Parliament Secretariat after the meeting. The committee was briefed on the activities of offices and agencies under the Ministry of Public Administration.

It advised all concerned to coordinate their activities at the field level to implement the 31-point reform agenda for state reform by bringing about a change in mindset.

Committee Chairman Sayeed Ahmed said that any legal, administrative or practical obstacles to implementing a decision must be brought to the committee’s attention. Necessary information, relevant documents and the actual circumstances must be presented without concealing anything.

He said public services must be made easier and faster, and accountability must be ensured. Digital services and the use of information technology can save citizens’ time, money and effort. Therefore, effective use of technology in service delivery must be ensured, and appropriate action must be taken against irregularities.

The committee chairman further said, “To solve problems, we must move beyond our traditional mindset and work with a spirit of accountability, transparency and cooperation. Do not forget that you are employees of the Republic. You do not belong to any party, individual or group. Do not consider this committee an adversary; it is a committee for all of us.”

The meeting was chaired by Sayeed Ahmed. Among the committee members who attended were State Minister for Public Administration Md Abdul Bari, ABM Ashraf Uddin (Nizan), Shahjahan Chowdhury, Amirul Islam Khan, Fakhr Uddin Ahmed, Rehena Akter and Md Nurul Islam.

item.title: Minister: Cyber police units to expand nationwide to combat digital crime
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has announced plans to expand the operations of the Cyber Police Unit across the country, covering central, divisional, district and upazila levels, to prevent and combat digital crime.
He said that expediting the delivery of justice requires various forms of analysis, evidence obtained through testing and proper certification. As the nature of crime evolves, plans are also underway to enhance the capabilities of law enforcement agencies to meet emerging challenges.
He made the remarks while inaugurating the newly constructed Cyber Police Center building and the digital forensic laboratory of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) in Chittagong on Wednesday.
Ambassador of the Republic of Korea to Bangladesh Kim Ji-jun, Sayed Al Noman, MP, Inspector General of Police (IGP) Md. Ali Hossain Fakir, Additional IGP (Headquarters) Sardar Nurul Amin and Additional IGP (CID) Barrister Mohammad Mosharraf Hossain were present at the ceremony, along with senior administrative officials, including Chittagong Divisional Commissioner Dr Mohammad Ziauddin, CMP Commissioner Hasan Mohammad Shawkat Ali and District Superintendent of Police Masud Alam.
Noting that the nature of crime has changed in the modern world, the Home Minister said many crimes are now committed in cyberspace, ranging from various forms of fraud to financial crimes such as stock market manipulation.
“There is no alternative to a digital forensic laboratory for preventing and combating these crimes,” he said.
He said plans for a police cyber unit had been in place from the outset and that its operations officially began on October 1. The unit currently operates under an Additional Inspector General. The newly inaugurated digital forensic laboratory will function under the supervision of the CID. Relevant departments will continue to cooperate in digital forensic analysis and testing, as they all fall under the same ministry.
“Under the leadership of the Cyber Police Unit, we will take steps to strengthen digital analysis capabilities at every level, from the central level to the divisions, districts and upazilas,” the Home Minister said.
He added that plans were also underway to establish Cyber Police Unit laboratories at the district and divisional levels to operate as digital forensic laboratories.
He noted that the CID had been operating chemical laboratories since its inception, issuing reports on various tests, including visceral analyses. “With changing times, expanding the capacity and scope of these laboratories has become essential,” he said.
Salahuddin Ahmed said the Government of the Republic of Korea and the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) had provided full support for the construction of the newly inaugurated building and the digital forensic laboratory in Chittagong. He thanked the Korean government, the Korean ambassador, KOICA representatives and the visiting Korean delegation for their support.
“Law enforcement agencies will be equipped with the necessary capabilities to prevent and combat crime in the modern digital world. To this end, all necessary preparations will be made, including laboratory facilities, essential equipment and other support resources, Insha'Allah,” he said.
CID sources said the department had taken steps to strengthen the police force's technical and investigative capabilities to combat cybercrime in key regions of the country, including Chittagong under the project titled “Safer Cyberspace for Digital Bangladesh.”
As online banking, mobile financial services, e-commerce and digital payment systems continue to expand, financial fraud, illicit transactions and attempts to conceal the origins of funds are also on the rise.

item.description:

Earlier, the second session, also known as the budget session, was prorogued on July 15 after 27 working days. During that session, Parliament passed the Tk938,000-crore national budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year, the first budget under the current BNP government.

item.title: Bangladesh plans 442MW solar plant in Rampal at estimated cost of Tk2,500 crore
item.description:
The government plans to build a 442-megawatt (MW) solar power plant in Rampal, Bagerhat, at an estimated cost of Tk2,500 crore, using existing land near the coal-fired power plant without acquiring additional land.
The project is expected to be completed by 2030 and will cover approximately 685 acres in Block B of Rampal. Electricity is expected to enter the national grid through existing transmission infrastructure serving the nearby coal-fired power complex, according to sources familiar with the proposal.
Planning Commission information shows that the project was included in the green pages of the Annual Development Program (ADP). A ministry source said it had received approval from the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) and was awaiting Cabinet Division approval before a government order could be issued.
The government initially plans to finance the project from its own resources, although assistance from development partners may be considered later.
The proposed facility could expand utility-scale renewable energy generation in a region associated with coal-based electricity. However, the solar project does not, by itself, signal the closure or replacement of the existing coal-fired power plant.
At an estimated Tk2,500 crore for 442MW of capacity, the project’s initial investment amounts to approximately Tk5.66 crore per MW. Its final economic viability will depend on electricity generation, procurement costs, maintenance, grid integration and equipment replacement.
Dr Khondaker Golam Moazzem, research director at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), told Dhaka Tribune that shifting from coal-based planning toward solar power represented a significant political and economic change. He stressed the importance of assessing generation costs and ensuring timely, quality implementation.
Dr Ijaz Hossain, former professor and dean of the Faculty of Engineering at Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET), said using government-owned land for solar power was a positive approach, given Bangladesh’s land scarcity and the need to expand domestic energy sources.
Using existing land and transmission infrastructure could reduce some development costs. However, the government needs to disclose the detailed project cost, procurement arrangements, financing structure and expected cost of electricity to establish its long-term value.
The construction schedule, procurement process and commissioning timeline have yet to be independently confirmed.
The project’s location makes environmental safeguards particularly important because Rampal is near the Sundarbans, one of the world’s largest mangrove forests.
Solar power produces substantially less direct air pollution during operation than coal-fired generation. However, large installations can still affect land use, drainage, habitats and local ecosystems, particularly during construction.
Professor Adil Mohammed Khan, executive director of the Institute for Planning and Development (IPD) and a faculty member at Jahangirnagar University, told Dhaka Tribune that solar expansion could benefit the environment and the Sundarbans if the project included life-cycle planning for the reuse and safe disposal of panels and batteries.
The government should make the project’s environmental impact assessment, Department of Environment clearance, site boundaries and distance from protected areas publicly available.
After solar plant approval in very recent meeting at ECNEC, chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, approved the project subject to eight-hour battery storage, requiring a revised DPP to determine the final cost; electricity generation costs were previously estimated at Tk6 per unit without storage and Tk9 with four-hour storage.
The environmental impact assessment (EIA) and required environmental clearances are currently under way, according to the information provided.
Planning State Minister Md Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki said: “Ensuring the economic viability, timely implementation and environmental protection of the Rampal solar power project is important for the government.”
Environmental responsibilities will continue beyond the plant’s commissioning. Solar panels, inverters and other electrical equipment will eventually require maintenance, replacement, recycling or safe disposal.
Panels commonly operate for around 25 years or longer, while battery lifespans vary according to technology and operating conditions.
If batteries are included in the Rampal project, the government should clarify their technology, replacement schedule and end-of-life management arrangements. Responsibilities for recycling and disposal should also be established, alongside the associated costs.
The proposed 442MW plant could strengthen Bangladesh’s renewable energy capacity while making use of existing land and infrastructure. Its success, however, will depend on transparent spending, reliable grid integration, timely implementation and credible environmental safeguards.

item.title: Police issue security guidelines for Durga Puja celebrations
item.description:
Police headquarters on Wednesday issued a set of security guidelines for organizers, visitors and others concerned to ensure safe, peaceful and festive celebrations of Sharadiya Durga Puja.
The police advised people not to spread rumors or share unverified information on social media, urging them to verify the authenticity of any information before liking, commenting on or sharing it.
To ensure security at puja mandaps, organizers have been advised to arrange separate entry and exit points for male and female visitors and discourage people from entering the mandaps with bags, sacks or bundles.
The police also recommended installing CCTV cameras and fire extinguishers at puja mandaps, setting up archway gates at important mandaps, and ensuring adequate lighting at the mandaps and idol immersion sites.
Where possible, organizers should also arrange standby generators or rechargeable lights.
Volunteers should be deployed to ensure security at puja mandaps. They should be provided with distinctive clothing, visible identity cards and armbands bearing the word ‘Volunteer’ so that they can be easily identified.
The police urged everyone to respect the religious sentiments of people belonging to other faiths and maintain communal harmony during the celebrations.
The use of sound systems should be restricted at puja mandaps near mosques during azan and prayers, as well as during idol immersion, the advisory said.
People were also advised to refrain from setting off fireworks and firecrackers during the celebrations.
To ensure the normal movement of vehicles, the police asked organizers and participants to follow designated routes during idol immersion and complete the process at locations specified by the local administration.

People can also call the national emergency service 999, which operates round the clock and is toll-free, to seek assistance from the police, ambulance services and fire service in an emergency.
